“Just a tick.”

“Where did you get it?”

“Out in the woods.”

“What would you take for it?”

“I don’t know. I don’t want to sell it.”

“All right. It’s a very small tick anyway.”

“Oh, anyone can find fault with a tick that isn’t theirs. I’m happy with it. It’s good enough for me.”

“Come on, there are plenty of ticks. I could get a thousand if I wanted.”

“Well, why don’t you? Because you know you can’t. This one’s early in the season, I think. It’s the first I’ve seen this year.”

“Say, Huck—I’ll give you my tooth for it.”

“Let me see.”

Tom took out a piece of paper and carefully unrolled it. Huckleberry looked at the tooth with longing. He was strongly tempted. Finally he said:

“Is it real?”

Tom lifted his lip and showed the empty space.

“Well, all right,” said Huckleberry. “It’s a deal.”

Tom put the tick into the small percussion-cap box that had recently held the pinchbug. The boys went their separate ways, both feeling richer than before.

When Tom reached the small wooden schoolhouse standing by itself, he walked quickly inside, acting as though he had hurried there as fast as he honestly could. He hung his hat on a peg and dropped into his seat, looking ready for work. The teacher sat high up in his large armchair with its woven wooden seat. The sleepy murmur of studying had made him doze off. Tom’s arrival woke him.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom knew that hearing his whole name meant trouble.

“Sir!”

“Come here. Now, sir, why are you late again, as usual?”

Tom was about to tell a lie when he noticed two long yellow braids hanging down a familiar back. Love made him recognize the girl instantly. Beside her was the only empty seat on the girls’ side of the schoolhouse. At once he said:

“I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!”

The teacher was so shocked that his pulse seemed to stop. He stared, unable to respond. The hum of studying died away. The pupils wondered whether this reckless boy had lost his mind. The teacher said:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.”

There was no misunderstanding those words.

“Thomas Sawyer, that is the most astonishing confession I’ve ever heard. A beating with the ruler won’t be enough for this. Take off your jacket.”

The teacher struck him with switches until his arm grew tired and he had used up a good part of his supply. Then came the order:

“Now, sir, go and sit with the girls! And let that teach you a lesson.”

Laughter spread through the room. Tom seemed embarrassed by it, but his real embarrassment came more from his awed admiration for the girl he did not yet know, and from the nervous happiness of his wonderful good luck.

The surrounding oaks sheltered a colony of nightingales—and I am there again now, with Idris beside me in the lovely springtime of her youth. Remember that I am only twenty-two, and the woman I love has scarcely seen seventeen summers. Swollen by autumn rain, the river has flooded the low ground, and Adrian, in his favourite boat, is amusing himself with the dangerous task of taking the highest branch from a submerged oak. Adrian, are you tired of living, that you should play so lightly with danger?

He has secured his prize and steers his boat through the flood. We watched him anxiously, but the current swept him away from us. He had to land much farther downstream and take a long way round before he could reach us. “He’s safe!” Idris said as he sprang ashore and waved the branch above his head to show his success. “We’ll wait for him here.”

We were alone. The sun had set, and the nightingales had begun to sing. The evening star shone clearly in the wash of light still lingering in the west. My angelic girl’s blue eyes rested on that gentle image of herself. “How the light pulses,” she said, “the light that is the star’s life. Its trembling radiance seems to tell us that its existence, like ours on earth, is uncertain and changeable. I imagine that it feels fear, and that it loves.”

“Don’t gaze at the star, my dear, generous friend,” I cried. “Don’t read love in its trembling light, or look towards distant worlds, or speak of a feeling that exists only in imagination. I have been silent so long. For so long I have ached to speak to you, to place my soul, my life, my whole being in your hands. Don’t look at the star, my love—or look, and let that eternal spark speak for me. Let it be my witness and my advocate, shining without a word. Love is to me what light is to that star. As long as its light is not extinguished by destruction, I will love you.”

The joy of that moment must remain forever hidden from the world’s unfeeling gaze. I still feel her graceful body pressed against my overflowing heart. Even now, the memory of that first kiss makes my sight falter, my pulse weaken, and my breath fail. Slowly, without speaking, we went to meet Adrian, whose approach we could hear.

I begged Adrian to come back to me after taking his sister home. That same evening, as we walked along the moonlit forest paths, I opened my whole heart to my friend, sharing its ecstasy and its hope. For a moment he looked troubled. “I should have seen this coming,” he said. “What conflict there will be now!

“Now, the most frequent letter in English is e. After that, the order is: a o i d h n r s t u y c f g l m w b k p q x z. E is so dominant that you rarely find a sentence of any length in which it is not the most common letter.

“So, right at the outset, we have a basis for something better than guesswork. The general usefulness of this table is obvious, although we will need only a little of its help with this particular cipher. Since 8 is our most frequent character, we can begin by assuming that it stands for e in the ordinary alphabet. To test that assumption, let us see whether 8 often appears twice in succession. English frequently doubles e—in words such as ‘meet,’ ‘fleet,’ ‘speed,’ ‘seen,’ ‘been,’ ‘agree,’ and so on. Here, despite the cipher’s short length, we find 8 doubled at least five times.

“Let us therefore take 8 to mean e. Now, ‘the’ is the most common word in the language. We should look for repeated groups of three characters, always in the same order, with 8 as the last character. If we find such groups, they will very probably stand for ‘the.’ Looking through the cipher, we discover at least seven examples of the group ;48. We can therefore suppose that ; stands for t, 4 for h, and 8 for e—the last identification now having strong support. We have made substantial progress.

“But identifying one word also allows us to establish something enormously useful: where several other words begin and end. Take, for example, the second-to-last appearance of ;48, not far from the cipher’s end. We know that the ; immediately after it begins another word. Of the six characters following this ‘the,’ we already know five. Let us write those characters out using the letters they represent, with a space left for the one we do not yet know:

t eeth.

“We can immediately rule out the final ‘th’ as part of the word that starts with the first t. Trying every letter of the alphabet in the empty space shows that no word can be formed that includes that ‘th.’ This leaves us with:

t ee,

and, if we work through the alphabet again as needed, we reach ‘tree’ as the only possible reading.
